newsitem.title: USA: Justice distances itself from Thompson charge.
newsitem.headline: Justice distances itself from Thompson charge.

text.p: The U.S. Justice Department has distanced itself from Republican Sen. Fred Thompson's charge that high-level Chinese officials plotted to increase their influence over the U.S. political process.

Thompson opened a Senate probe on campaign fundraising on Tuesday with a sweeping accusation that "the committee believes that high-level Chinese government officials crafted a plan to increase China's influence over the U.S. political process."
He said his view was based on confidential documents, many of which were provided by the Justice Department.

But the Justice Department, in a letter to the Tennessee senator quoted on ABC's "This Week" program, said: "You neither requested nor received assessments of the accuracy of any conclusions you drew from information available to the committee."
"Those conclusions of course are your own," said the letter, signed by Assistant Attorney General Andrew Fois.

U.S. News & World Report magazine on Sunday quoted the FBI as suggesting a crucial link was missing between alleged Chinese efforts to exert influence and Democratic Party efforts to raise money from Asians.

"There was a campaign by the Chinese to infiltrate Congress and a campaign by the Democrats to gain contributions from wealthy Asian-Americans," the magazine quoted the FBI official as saying. "Were the two linked? Where's the proof?"
A key focus of the Senate investigation has been John Huang, who raised money for the Democratic Party -- much of which had to be returned because it violated rules or laws.

Thompson's committee has been asked to consider granting Huang immunity from prosecution so he can testify before it. But the committee has been reluctant to grant immunity because such grants have sometimes interefered with past prosecutions.

Newsweek reported on Sunday that Huang allegedly funneled illegal foreign contributions to the Democrats as long ago as 1992. "The paper trail dates back to Aug. 18, 1992, just a few weeks after Bill Clinton was first nominated for president," the weekly magazine said in its latest edition.

Senate investigators have uncovered documents showing that on the day an obscure California real estate company called Hip Hing Holdings made a $50,000 contribution to the Democratic National Committee, a similar amount was wired into the company's U.S. bank account from the Jakarta headquarters of the Lippo Group, Newsweek said.
Huang was the top representative in Los Angeles for the Lippo Group, an Indonesian financial and real estate conglomerate owned by the Riady family, which is also under campaign finance scrutiny.
Time magazine reported on Sunday that an Arkansas lawyer, Joe Giroir, played a more pivotal role in the Lippo Group's quest for influence in Washington than Huang.

Time said the Riady family formed a partnership with Giroir, former managing partner in the Rose Law Firm where first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton worked, to line up U.S. investors for the family's Asian ventures.
